Recombining Permutations

PermutationsParityInvariants
Game: Numbers stand on a circle and arrows show where a shuffle sends each one. Swap two numbers and watch the loops of arrows split or join.
How to play: Press one number, then another one, to swap them. Count the loops before and after.

Look for the math

Put the numbers 1, ..., N on a circle and draw an arrow from each number to the number it is sent to. Following the arrows round, you come back where you started: the loops are the cycles of the permutation. A number that stays put is a loop of length one.

Swapping two numbers

Pressing a and then b multiplies the permutation by the transposition (a b): the two arrows that leave a and b trade their targets. The number of loops changes by exactly one. If a and b were in the same loop it splits into two; if they were in different loops, the two loops join into one.

The test tried this on every permutation of up to 8 numbers and every pair: 100% of the swaps changed the count by one, in the direction just described.

Even and odd, and the Fifteen

Because every swap changes the number of loops by one, it also changes whether N minus the number of loops is even or odd. That is the parity of the permutation, and it flips at every swap. This is the idea behind the Fifteen puzzle: each move swaps the blank with a tile, so after an odd number of moves the permutation is odd.

Start with N = 4 and try to reach the picture where every number has only a loop of length one. How many swaps do you need at least?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
